title: Fundamental Rights and Judicial Review Explained

scenes.text: Can the government take away your basic rights?
scenes.narration: Can Parliament pass any law it wants, or is someone watching? Here's the secret: the Constitution gives you shield walls and gives judges a magnifying glass!

scenes.text: Fundamental rights are boundary ropes; judicial review is the umpire.
scenes.narration: Think of this like a cricket match. Fundamental rights are boundary lines the bowler cannot cross, while judicial review acts like the third umpire checking if a delivery is illegal.

scenes.heading: Limiting State Sovereignty
scenes.narration: Fundamental rights come from natural rights, meaning the state confirms your freedom rather than granting it. This tilts power toward individuals by checking arbitrary state power.

scenes.heading: Amendments Shielding Property Laws
scenes.narration: When property rights clashed with land reforms, Parliament added the Ninth Schedule in nineteen fifty-one to shield laws from courts. Later amendments protected directive policies too.

scenes.heading: Doctrines of Judicial Review
items: Severability removes only invalid legal sections
Eclipse places unconstitutional provisions under shadow
Judicial review originates from American Marbury case
scenes.narration: Borrowed from America's Marbury versus Madison case, judicial review lets Indian courts inspect laws. Under severability, judges cut out only the bad part of a law, saving the rest.

scenes.heading: Procedural vs Substantive Due Process
scenes.narration: Here is the difference: procedural due process checks if officials follow fair steps, like commuting delayed death sentences in Shatrugan Chauhan. Substantive due process questions the law's fairness itself.

items: Fundamental rights limit arbitrary state sovereignty
Ninth Schedule shielded early property laws
Judicial review checks executive action and laws
scenes.narration: Remember these three rules: rights protect individual freedom, amendments shielded property reforms from judicial review, and courts examine both government procedures and the wisdom of laws.
